title: Three kinds of seeing and doing
hookLine: the three gunas shape how you see, how you act and who you are while doing it
carry: the three gunas color how you see and act
last: THE DOER IS ONE CAUSE OF FIVE.

cards: On the first morning, Arjuna asked Krishna to drive the chariot between the two armies, so he could see who he'd be fighting.
He looked across and saw them one by one: grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, friends. Each face belonged to a side, mine or theirs. That's when he fell apart.
For seventeen chapters, Krishna has been teaching him another way to see. Today, in chapter eighteen, he sorts seeing itself, then doing, then the doer, by the three gunas, the threads of nature.

teach.h: SEEING ONE, SEEING MANY, SEEING A BIT.
teach.b: Knowledge first. Verse twenty: sattvic knowledge sees one undying reality in all beings, undivided in the divided. It's chapter thirteen's one light, the seeing Arjuna lacked on that first morning.
Verse twenty-one: rajasic knowledge sees all beings as separate, each its own thing, nothing connecting them.
Verse twenty-two: tamasic knowledge clings to one small piece as if it were everything, without reason, without grasping what's true. Then action.
Verse twenty-three: sattvic action is what needs doing, done without attachment, without craving or hate, by someone not chasing the fruit.

Verse twenty-four: rajasic action is driven by desire or ego, done with enormous strain. Verse twenty-five: tamasic action starts in confusion, with no thought for the consequences or the harm to others. Then the doer.
Verse twenty-six: the sattvic doer is free of attachment, doesn't talk about themselves, is full of steadiness and energy, and unchanged by success or failure.
Verse twenty-seven: the rajasic doer is passionate, wants the fruit, is greedy, can be harmful, and swings between joy and grief.

Verse twenty-eight: the tamasic doer is unsteady, stubborn, lazy, gloomy, and dirghasutri. That last word is a compound of dirgha, long, and sutra, thread. Long-threaded: someone who keeps stretching a job out.
A procrastinator, sitting right there in the Gita's last chapter. The chapter goes on to sort understanding, resolve and happiness the same way.

teach.h: THREE GUNAS, THREE WAYS TO SEE.
teach.b: This is the Hindu teaching of the gunas: sattva, clear; rajas, restless; tamas, heavy. Every person has all three, and they shift. As many teachers read it, the point isn't to label yourself.
It's to notice which thread is pulling now, and lean toward sattva.

how: Some Hindu teachers use Gita 18.19–18.28 as a mirror for work and study: aiming for sattvic knowledge, action and doing, steady, unattached and unshaken by success or failure.

o: a thread worn by priests for long life
someone who keeps dragging a task out
a sage who chants a very long sutra

games.q: three kinds each — tap the pairs.
p: one piece taken for the whole

s: the sattvic doer is unchanged by success or failure
verse 26: steady, energetic, free of attachment and self-talk.
the Gita praises action done with enormous strain as the highest
verse 24: action driven by desire or ego, with great strain, is rajasic.
the Gita has a word for procrastinator

games.q: you see that everyone on your team is part of one project, and you do your part without needing credit. which kind is that?
games.why: sattvic: seeing the one in the many (verse 20), and acting without attachment to the fruit (verse 23).

practice: Think of one task waiting for you, and notice, without judgment, how you're seeing it: part of something bigger, only your piece, or one annoying detail? Notice, too, how you'd do it: steadily, frantically, or not at all yet.
Then picture doing it the steady way, with energy but without needing praise, and hold that picture for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Dirghasutri, long-threaded, one who drags a task out. Gita eighteen, nineteen to twenty-eight: knowledge, action and the doer each come in three kinds, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, and the tamasic doer is dirghasutri.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dirghasutri, long-threaded (dirgha, long + sutra, thread): the one who drags a task out; Gita 18.28.

carryVoice: Your line: the three gunas color how you see and act. Notice the thread, then lean toward sattva. On to day two hundred twenty-two tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.21–1.26 (Arjuna asks to see the armies and sees his kin)
